nodes.name: submodular set function
nodes.statement: A set function $f:2^{\sensors}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is called \emph{submodular} if, for all $\cA\subseteq\cB\subseteq\sensors$ and $s\in\sensors\setminus \cB$ it holds that $f(\cA\cup\{s\})-f(\cA)\geq f(\cB\cup\{s\})-f(\cB)$.
nodes.statement_short: A set function has diminishing returns: the marginal gain of adding $s$ never grows as the base set grows.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Offline Sensor Selection Problem
differentia: for all $\cA\subseteq\cB\subseteq\sensors$ and $s\in\sensors\setminus \cB$ it holds that $f(\cA\cup\{s\})-f(\cA)\geq f(\cB\cup\{s\})-f(\cB)$

nodes.name: mean squared prediction error
nodes.statement: One way to quantify the predictive uncertainty is the mean squared prediction error, $$\MSE(\cX_{\sensors\setminus\cA}\mid \bx_{\cA}) = \frac{1}{\numsensors}\sum_{s\in\sensors\setminus\cA} \mathbb{E}[(\cX_s-\mathbb{E}[\cX_{s}\mid\bx_{\cA}])^{2}\mid \bx_{\cA}].$$
nodes.statement_short: Average conditional squared prediction error at the unobserved locations given the measurements $\bx_{\cA}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Offline Sensor Selection Problem

nodes.name: expected mean squared prediction error (EMSE)
nodes.statement: Thus, we can base our optimization on the \emph{expected mean squared prediction error}, $$\EMSE(\cA) = \int dp(\bx_{\cA}) \MSE(\cX_{\sensors\setminus\cA}\mid \bx_{\cA}).$$
nodes.statement_short: MSE averaged over the not-yet-observed measurements of the selected set $\cA$.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Offline Sensor Selection Problem

nodes.name: reduction in mean squared prediction error $\fEMSE$
nodes.statement: Equivalently, we can maximize the \emph{reduction} in mean squared prediction error, $$\fEMSE(\cA) = \EMSE(\emptyset)-\EMSE(\cA).$$
nodes.statement_short: The utility of a sensor set, defined as the EMSE it removes relative to selecting nothing.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Offline Sensor Selection Problem

nodes.name: regret and no-regret
nodes.statement: The difference between this quantity and what our protocol obtains is known as its \emph{regret}, and an algorithm is said to be \emph{no-regret} if its average regret tends to zero (or less)\footnote{Formally, if $R_T$ is the total regret for the first $T$ rounds, no-regret means $\limsup_{T \to \infty} R_T/T \le 0$.} as $T \to \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Regret is the shortfall against the best fixed $\K$-set; an algorithm is no-regret if average regret vanishes.
nodes.section: 2.2 The Online Sensor Selection Problem

nodes.name: $(1-1/e)$-regret and no-$(1-1/e)$-regret
nodes.statement: We therefore define the $(1-1/e)$-regret of a sequence of (possibly random) sets $\set{S_t}_{t=1}^T$ as \vspace{-0.5em} \[ \regret_{T} := \paren{1-1/e} \cdot \max_{S \subseteq \sensors: |S| \le \K} \sum_{t=1}^T \obj_t(S) \ - \ \sum_{t=1}^T \E{\obj_t(S_t)} \] where the expectation is taken over the distribution for each $S_t$. We say an online algorithm producing a sequence of sets has \emph{no-$(1-1/e)$-regret} if $\limsup_{T \to \infty} \frac{\regret_{T}}{T} \le 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Regret measured against a $(1-1/e)$-discounted offline optimum, the best any efficient algorithm can target.
nodes.section: 2.2 The Online Sensor Selection Problem

nodes.name: induced sampling distribution $\psamp$
nodes.statement: For a sampling procedure with input distribution $p$, we let $\psamp$ denote the resulting distribution, where in all cases at most one sensor is selected, and nothing is selected with probability $1-\sum_{\sensor} \psamp_{\sensor}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\psamp$ is the distribution a sampling protocol actually realizes, allowing an explicit no-selection outcome.

nodes.name: activation-probability map $\rho(x,y)$
nodes.statement: Let \[ \rho(x, y) := (1-\gamma)\frac{x}{y} + \frac{\gamma}{\numsensors}\mbox{.} \]
nodes.statement_short: The $\gamma$-mixed weight-to-probability map.

nodes.name: threshold-selection game
nodes.statement: We construct a particular game that the sensors play, where the strategies are the thresholds (suitably discretized), there is an \emph{activation cost} $\actcost_{\sensor}$ that $\sensor$ pays if $\estimate{\payoff}_{\sensor} \ge \thresh_{\sensor}$, and the payoffs are defined as follows: Let $\payoff_{\sensor} = \obj_{t}(S\cup \{v\})-\obj_{t}(S)$ be the marginal benefit of selecting $\sensor$ given that sensor set $S$ has already been selected. Let $A$ be the set of sensors that activate in the current iteration of the game, and let $\paymaxact{\sensor} := \max \paren{\payoff_{\sensor'} : \sensor' \in A \setminus \set{\sensor}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Sensors play a game whose strategies are activation thresholds, paying an activation cost when they report.
nodes.section: 6 Observation-Dependent Sampling

nodes.name: reward function $\gpay_{\sensor}(\thresh)$ of the threshold game
nodes.statement: The particular reward function $\gpay_{\sensor}$ we choose for each sensor $\sensor$ for each iteration of the game is \[ \gpay_{\sensor}(\thresh) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \actcost_{\sensor} - \max\paren{\payoff_{\sensor} - \paymaxact{\sensor}, 0} & \text{if }\estimate{\payoff} < \thresh\\ \max\paren{\payoff_{\sensor} - \paymaxact{\sensor}, 0} - \actcost_{\sensor} & \text{if }\estimate{\payoff} \ge \thresh \end{array} \right. \]
nodes.statement_short: A sensor's reward is its marginal benefit over the best other active sensor, minus its activation cost, signed by whether it activated.
nodes.section: 6 Observation-Dependent Sampling

nodes.name: offline greedy output $\gout(f)$
nodes.statement: if we let $\gout(f)$ be the result of running the offline greedy algorithm on the problem \[\argmax\set{f(S) : S \subset \sensors,\ |S| \le \K}\]
nodes.statement_short: $\gout(f)$ denotes the set the offline greedy algorithm returns for the cardinality-constrained maximization of $f$.
nodes.section: 6 Observation-Dependent Sampling

nodes.name: Offline sensor selection problem
nodes.statement: However, in practice, we would like to only select a small set of, e.g., at most $k$ sensors due to bandwidth and power constraints: $$\cA^*=\argmax_{\cA}\fEMSE(\cA)\text{ s.t. }|\cA|\leq k.$$
nodes.statement_short: Choose at most $k$ sensors maximizing the EMSE reduction $\fEMSE$.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Offline Sensor Selection Problem

nodes.name: Online sensor selection problem
nodes.statement: Our goal is to maximize the total reward obtained by the system over $T$ rounds, $\sum_{t=1}^T \obj_t(S_t)$.
nodes.section: 2.2 The Online Sensor Selection Problem

nodes.name: Distributed one-element sampling problem
nodes.statement: The key challenge in developing a distributed version of \EXPthree is to find a way to sample exactly one element from a probability distribution $p$ over sensors in a distributed manner.
nodes.statement_short: Sample exactly one sensor from a prescribed distribution $p$ without any central coordinator.
nodes.section: 4.1 Distributed Selection of a Single Sensor

nodes.name: Assumptions of the broadcast model
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate}\denselist \item Each sensor $\sensor \in \sensors$ is able to compute its contribution to the utility $\obj_{t}(S\cup \{\sensor\})-\obj_{t}(S)$, where $S$ are a subset of sensors that have already been selected. \item Each sensor can broadcast to all other sensors. \item The sensors have calibrated clocks and unique, linearly ordered identifiers. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Each sensor can compute its own marginal utility, can broadcast to all sensors, and has a calibrated clock and unique ordered ID.
nodes.section: 4 Distributed Algorithm for Online Sensor Selection

nodes.name: Assumptions of the star network model
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate}\denselist \item Every sensor stores its probability mass $p_\sensor$ with it, and can only send messages to and receive messages from the base station. \item The base station is able, after receiving messages from a set $S$ of sensors, to compute the utility $\obj_{t}(S)$ and send this utility back to the active sensors.
nodes.statement_short: Sensors talk only to a base station, which computes utilities and returns them to the active sensors.
nodes.section: 5 The Star Network Model

nodes.name: Conditions on the bandit distribution $p_{\sensor}(t)$
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item $p_{\sensor}(t)$ can be computed from local information $\sensor$ possesses and global information the server has. \item There exists an $\epsilon > 0$ such that $p_{\sensor}(t) \ge \epsilon$ for all $t$. \item $p_{\sensor}(t) < p_{\sensor}(t+1)$ implies $\sensor$ was selected in round $t$. \item There exists $\hat{\epsilon} > 0$ such that $p_{\sensor}(t+1) \ge p_{\sensor}(t)/(1+\hat{\epsilon})$ for all $t$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Four conditions on a MAB algorithm's action distribution: local computability, a floor $\epsilon$, increases only after selection, and bounded per-round decay.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Guarantee of the PMS Protocol
nodes.statement: \begin{prop} Fix any fixed $p$ and $\alpha>0$. The \LimitProtocolShort always selects at most one sensor, ensures $$\forall \sensor:\ \prob{\sensor \text{ selected}} = (1 - e^{-\alpha})p_{\sensor}$$ and requires no more than $\alpha$ messages in expectation. \end{prop}
nodes.statement_short: The PMS Protocol selects at most one sensor, selects $\sensor$ with probability exactly $(1-e^{-\alpha})p_{\sensor}$, and costs $\le\alpha$ messages.

assumptions: Fix any fixed $p$ and $\alpha>0$.
conclusions: The \LimitProtocolShort always selects at most one sensor

nodes.name: Distributed single sensor selection in the broadcast model
nodes.statement: \begin{theorem} In the broadcast model, running \EXPthree using the \LimitProtocolShort with $\alpha = 1$, and rerunning the protocol whenever nothing is selected, yields exactly the same regret bound as standard \EXPthree, and in each round at most $e/(e-1)+2 \approx 3.582$ messages are broadcast in expectation. \end{theorem}
nodes.statement_short: EXP3 driven by the PMS Protocol ($\alpha=1$, rerun on empty) keeps EXP3's regret at about $3.582$ broadcasts per round.

nodes.name: Performance of the Distributed Online Greedy (DOG) algorithm
nodes.statement: \begin{theorem} The \algoname algorithm selects, at each round $t$ a set $S_{t}\subseteq\sensors$ of $k$ sensors such that \[ \frac{1}{T}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(S_{t})\right]\geq \frac{1-\frac{1}{e}}{T}\max_{|S|\leq k} \sum_{t=1}^{T} f_{t}(S) - O\left(k\sqrt{\frac{n\log n}{T}}\right). \] In expectation, only $\cO(k)$ messages are exchanged each round. \end{theorem}
nodes.statement_short: DOG attains the $(1-1/e)$ offline optimum up to $O(k\sqrt{n\log n/T})$ average regret with $\cO(k)$ messages per round.

nodes.name: Message-optimal lazyDOG variant
nodes.statement: \begin{theorem} The variant of \lazydog that runs the \LimitProtocol$(\alpha)$ with lazy renormalization for $\K' := \ceil{\K/(1 - e^{-\alpha})}$ stages, but does not rerun it if nothing is selected in a given stage, has the following guarantees: ($1$) the number of sensors that activate each round in \lazydog is at most $\K' (\alpha + e -1)$ in expectation and $\cO(\alpha\K\log n)$ with high probability, ($2$) the number of messages is at most twice the number of activations, ($3$) the expected number of sensors selected in each round is at most $\K'$ and $(4)$ its $\paren{1 - 1/e}$-regret is at most $\K' / \K$ times that of \dog. \end{theorem}

nodes.name: OG_unit with faulty actions
nodes.statement: \begin{theorem} Fix finite set $\sensors$, $\K \in \nats$, and a sequence of monotone submodular functions $f_1, \ldots, f_T:2^{\sensors} \to [0,1]$. Let $\OPT_{\K} = \max_{S \subset \sensors, |S| \le \K} \sum_{t=1}^{t} f_t(S)$. For all $\sensor \in \sensors$ let $\sensor'$ be a random element which is $v$ with probability $1-\delta_\sensor$ and is $\NULL$\footnote{Here, a $\NULL$ element always contributes nothing in the way of utility, so that $f_t(S \cup \set{\NULL}) = f_t(S)$ for all $t$ and $S$.} with probability $\delta_\sensor$. Let $f'_t(S') := \E{f_t(S)}$ where $S$ the set obtained by including every element $\sensor'$ of $S'$ in it independently with probability $\delta_{\sensor}$. Let $S'_1, \ldots, S'_T$ be the sequence of random sets obtained from running \OGunit with actions $\sensors' := \set{\sensor' : \sensor \in V}$ and objective functions $\set{f'_t}_{t = 1}^T$ and $\K' = \K/(1-\delta)$ stages, where $\delta = \max_{\sensor} \delta_{\sensor}$. nodes.name: Remark on sensors' estimates of the network size $n$
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Remark} Running our variant of \EXPthree requires that each sensor know the number of sensors, $n$, in order to compute its activation probability. If each sensor $\sensor$ has only a reasonable estimate of $n_{\sensor}$ of $n$, however, our algorithm still performs well. For example, it is possible to prove that if all of the sensors have the same estimate $n_{\sensor} = cn$ for some constant $c > 0$, then the upper bound on expected regret, $R(c)$, grows as $R(c) \approx R(1)\cdot \max \set{c, 1/c}$. The expected number of activations in this case increases by at most $\paren{\frac{1}{c} - 1}\gamma$. In general underestimating $n$ leads to more activations, and underestimating or overestimating $n$ can lead to more regret. This graceful degradation of performance with respect to the error in estimating $n$ holds for all of our algorithms.
nodes.statement_short: If all sensors use the same estimate $cn$ of $n$, regret degrades only by a factor $\max\set{c,1/c}$.

nodes.name: Contrast with leader election and random-walk sampling
nodes.statement: This problem is distinct from randomized leader election \cite{Nakano02}, where the objective is to select exactly one element but the element need not be drawn from a specified distribution. We note that under the multi-hop communication model, sampling one element from the uniform distribution given a rooted spanning tree can be done via a simple random walk~\cite{Kuhn08}, but that under the broadcast and star network models this approach degenerates to centralized sampling. Our algorithm, in contrast, samples from an arbitrary distribution by allowing sensors to individually decide to activate. Our bottom-up approach also has two other advantages: ($1$) it is amenable to modification of the activation probabilities based on local observations, as we discuss in~\secref{sec:measure-dependent-sampling}, and ($2$) since it does not rely on any global state of the network such as a spanning tree, it can gracefully cope with significant edge or node failures.
nodes.statement_short: Unlike leader election or spanning-tree random walks, the bottom-up scheme samples from an arbitrary distribution and needs no global state.

nodes.name: EXP3
nodes.statement: \EXPthree works as follows: It is parameterized by a \emph{learning rate} $\eta$, and an \emph{exploration probability} $\gamma$. It maintains a set of weights $w_{s}$, one for each arm (sensor) $s$, initialized to 1. At every round $t$, it will select each arm $s$ with probability $$p_{s}=(1-\gamma)\frac{w_{s}}{\sum_{s'} w_{s'}}+\frac{\gamma}{\numsensors},$$ i.e., with probability $\gamma$ it explores, picking an arm uniformly at random, and with probability $(1-\gamma)$ it exploits, picking an arm $s$ with probability proportional to its weight $w_{s}$. Once an arm $s$ has been selected, a feedback $r=\obj_{t}(\{s\})$ is obtained, and the weight $w_{s}$ is updated to $$w_{s}\leftarrow w_{s}\exp(\eta r/p_{s}).$$

nodes.name: naive distributed sampling scheme
nodes.statement: A naive distributed algorithm would be to let each sensor keep track of all activation probabilities $p$. Then, one sensor (e.g., with the lowest identifier) would broadcast a single random number $u$ uniformly distributed in $[0,1]$, and the sensor $\sensor$ for which $\sum_{i=1}^{\sensor-1} p_{i} \le u < \sum_{i=1}^{\sensor} p_{i}$ would activate. However, for large sensor network deployments, this algorithm would require each sensor to store a large amount of global information (all activation probabilities $p$). Instead, each sensor $\sensor$ could store only their own probability mass $p_{\sensor}$; the sensors would then, in order of their identifiers, broadcast their probabilities $p_{\sensor}$, and stop once the sum of the probabilities exceeds $u$. This approach only requires a constant amount of local information, but requires an impractical $\Theta(n)$ messages to be sent, and sent sequentially over $\Theta(n)$ time steps.
nodes.statement_short: Broadcast one uniform $u$ and let the sensor whose CDF interval contains it activate; the local-storage variant needs $\Theta(n)$ sequential messages.

nodes.name: Distributed Online Greedy (DOG)
nodes.statement: \begin {algorithm*} \Titleofalgo { Distributed Online Greedy (\dog) \ \ (described in the broadcast model) } \KwIn { $\K \in \nats$, a set $\sensors$, and $\alpha, \gamma, \eta \in \reals_{>0}$. Reasonable defaults are any $\alpha \in [1, \ln |\sensors|]$, and $\gamma = \eta$ $=$ $\min\paren{1, \paren{|\sensors| \ln |\sensors|/g}^{1/2}}$, where $g$ is a guess for the maximum cumulative reward of any single sensor~\cite{auer02}. } Initialize $w_{\sensor, i} \gets 1$ and $Z_{\sensor,i} \gets |\sensors|$ for all $\sensor \in \sensors$, $i \in [\K]$. Let $\rho(x, y) := (1-\gamma)\frac{x}{y} + \frac{\gamma}{|\sensors|}$.\\ \For{ \KwEach \emph{round} $t = 1, 2, 3, \ldots $} { Initialize $S_{\sensor,t} \gets \emptyset$ for each $\sensor$ in parallel.\\ \For{ \KwEach \emph{stage} $i \in [\K]$} { \For{ \KwEach \emph{sensor} $\sensor \in \sensors$ \emph{in parallel}} { \Repeat {\emph{$\sensor$ receives a message of type } $\tuple{\emph{select } \id}$ } { Sample $X_{\sensor} \sim \Poisson{\alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\sensor,i}, Z_{\sensor,i})} $.\\ \If{$(X_{\sensor} \ge 1)$} { Broadcast $\tuple{\text{sampled } X_{\sensor}, \id(\sensor)}$; Receive messages from sensors $S$. (Include $\sensor \in S$ for convenience).\\ \If{$\id(\sensor) = \min_{\sensor' \in S} \id(\sensor')$}{ Select exactly one element $v_{it}$ from $S$ such that each $\sensor'$ is selected with probability $X_{\sensor'}/\sum_{u \in S} X_{u}$.\\ Broadcast $\tuple{\text{select } \id(\sensor_{it})}$.\\ } Receive message $\tuple{\text{select } \id(\sensor_{it})}$.\\ \If{$\id(\sensor) = \id(\sensor_{it})$}{ Observe $\obj_t(S_{\sensor,t} + \sensor)$; $\payoff \gets \obj_t(S_{\sensor,t} + \sensor) - \obj_t(S_{\sensor,t})$; $\Delta_{\sensor} \gets w_{\sensor,i} (\exp\set{\eta \cdot \payoff/ \rho(w_{\sensor,i}, Z_{\sensor,i})} - 1)$; $Z_{\sensor,i} \gets Z_{\sensor,i} + \Delta_{\sensor}$; $w_{\sensor} \gets w_{\sensor} + \Delta_{\sensor}$; Broadcast $\tuple{\text{weight update }\Delta_{\sensor}, \id(\sensor)}$.\\ } } \lIf{\emph{receive message $\tuple{\text{weight update }\Delta, \id(\sensor_{it})}$}}{ $S_{\sensor,t} \gets S_{\sensor,t} \cup \set{\sensor_{it}}$; $Z_{\sensor,i} \gets Z_{\sensor,i} + \Delta $;\\ } } } } } \vspace{2mm} \KwOut{At the end of each round $t$ each sensor has an identical local copy $S_{\sensor,t}$ of the selected set $S_{t}$.}
nodes.statement_short: Per-stage distributed EXP3 over $\K$ greedy stages: sensors Poisson-sample themselves, the min-ID sensor picks the winner, and weight updates are broadcast.

nodes.name: lazy renormalization scheme for EXP3
nodes.statement: Our lazy renormalization scheme for \EXPthree works as follows. Each sensor $\sensor$ maintains its weight $w_{\sensor}(t)$ and an estimate $Z_{\sensor}(t)$ for $Z(t) := \sum_{\sensor'}w_{\sensor'}(t)$, Initially, $w_{\sensor}(0) = 1$ and $Z_{\sensor}(0) = \numsensors$ for all $\sensor$. The central server stores $Z(t)$. Let \[ \rho(x, y) := (1-\gamma)\frac{x}{y} + \frac{\gamma}{\numsensors}\mbox{.} \] Each sensor then proceeds to activate as in the sampling procedure of~\secref{sec:sampling} as if its probability mass in round $t$ were $q_{\sensor} = \rho(w_{\sensor}(t), Z_{\sensor}(t))$ instead of its true value of $\rho(w_{\sensor}(t), Z(t))$. A single sensor is selected by the server with respect to the true value $Z(t)$, resulting in a selection from the desired distribution. Moreover, $\sensor$'s estimate $Z_{\sensor}(t)$ is only updated on rounds when it communicates with the server under these circumstances. This allows the estimated probabilities of all of the sensors to sum to more than one, but has the benefit of significantly reducing the communication cost in the star network model under certain assumptions. We call the result \emph{Distributed EXP3}, give its pseudocode for round $t$ in~\figref{fig:lazy-renorm-code}.
nodes.statement_short: Sensors act on a stale normalizer estimate $Z_{\sensor}(t)$ and refresh it only when they talk to the server, which selects using the true $Z(t)$.

nodes.name: Distributed EXP3
nodes.statement: \begin {algorithm}[tb] \Titleofalgo { Distributed \EXPthree (executing on round $t$)} \KwIn{Parameters $\alpha, \eta, \gamma \in \reals_{> 0}$, sensor set $\sensors$.} Let $\rho(x, y) := (1-\gamma)\frac{x}{y} + \frac{\gamma}{|\sensors|}$.\\ \emph{Sensors: } \\ \For {\KwEach \emph{sensor $\sensor$ in parallel}}{ Sample $r_{\sensor}$ uniformly at random from $[0,1]$.\\ \If {$(r_{\sensor} \ge 1 - \alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\sensor}(t), Z_{\sensor}(t))$}{ Send $\tuple{r_{\sensor}, w_{\sensor}(t)}$ to the server.\\ Receive message $\tuple{Z, w}$ from server.\\ $Z_{\sensor}(t+1) \gets Z$; $w_{\sensor}(t+1) \gets w$. \\ }\lElse{ $Z_{\sensor}(t+1) \gets Z_{\sensor}(t)$; $w_{\sensor}(t+1) \gets w_{\sensor}(t)$.\\ } } \emph{Server:}\\ Receive messages from a set $S$ of sensors. \\ \lIf{$S = \emptyset$}{Select nothing and wait for next round.} \lElse{ \For {\KwEach \emph{sensor} $\sensor \in S$}{ $Y_{\sensor} \gets \min \set{x : \prob{X \le x} \ge r_{\sensor}}$, where $X \sim \Poisson{\alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\sensor}(t),Z(t))}$.\\ Select $\sensor$ with probability $Y_{\sensor}/\sum_{\sensor' \in S} Y_{\sensor'}$.\\ Observe the payoff $\payoff$ for the selected sensor $\sensor^*$; $w_{\sensor^*}(t+1) \gets w_{\sensor^*}(t) \cdot \exp \set{\eta \payoff / \rho(w_{\sensor^*}(t),Z(t))}$; $Z(t+1) \gets Z(t) + w_{\sensor^*}(t+1) - w_{\sensor^*}(t)$\; \lFor{ \KwEach $\sensor \in S \setminus \sensor^*$}{ $w_{\sensor}(t+1) \gets w_{\sensor}(t)$\; } \lFor{ \KwEach $\sensor \!\in\! S$}{ Send $\tuple{Z(t\!+\!1), w_{\sensor}(t\!+\!1)}$ to $\sensor$.\\ } } }
nodes.statement_short: Each sensor sends a uniform draw and its weight when it clears a stale-normalizer threshold; the server inverts the draw into a Poisson sample and selects.

nodes.name: Proof of the broadcast-model single-sensor theorem
nodes.statement: \begin{proof}[of Theorem~\ref{thm:distributed-single-sensor-selection}] To prove the regret bounds, note that in every round the distribution over sensor selections in the variant of \EXPthree we describe (that uses the distributed multinomial sampling scheme and repeatedly reruns the protocol in order to always select some sensor in each round) is precisely the same as the original \EXPthree. Thus the regret bounds for \EXPthree~\cite{auer02} carry over unchanged. We next bound the number of broadcasts. Fix a round, and let $S$ set of sensors that activate in that round. The total number of broadcasts is then $|S|+2$; using their calibrated clocks, each sensor (re)samples $X_{\sensor} \sim \Poisson{\alpha p_{\sensor} }$ and activates if $X_{\sensor} \ge 1$. If no sensors activate before a specified timeout period, the default behavior is to rerun the sampling step. Eventually $|S| \ge 1$ sensors activate in the same period. A distinguished sensor in $S$ then determines the selected sensor $\sensor$, broadcasts $\id(\sensor)$, and $\sensor$ broadcasts its observed reward. We prove $\E{|S|} \le \alpha / (1 - e^{-\alpha})$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:broadcast-activations}. When $\alpha = 1$, this gives us the claimed bound on the number of broadcasts. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Direct argument: the induced selection distribution equals EXP3's, so regret carries over; then count $|S|+2$ broadcasts and bound $\E{|S|}$.

nodes.name: Proof of the expected-activations proposition
nodes.statement: \begin{proof} Let $X_{\sensor} \sim \Bernoulli{\alpha \cdot p_{\sensor}}$ be the indicator random variable for the activation of $\sensor$, and let $X := \sum_{\sensor} X_{\sensor}$. The expected number of sensor activations is then \[ \E{X \ |\ X \ge 1} = \E{X}/\prob{X \ge 1} \mbox{.} \] In the limit as $\max_{\sensor} p_{\sensor}$ tends to zero, $X$ converges to a Poisson random variable with mean $\alpha$. In this case, $\frac{\E{X}}{\prob{X \ge 1}} = \alpha / (1 - e^{-\alpha})$ To see that this is an upper bound, consider an arbitrary distribution $p$ on the sensors, and fix some $\sensor$ with $x := p_{\sensor} > 0$. We claim that replacing $\sensor$ with two sensors $\sensor_1$ and $\sensor_2$ with positive probability mass $x_1$ and $x_2$ with $x = x_1+x_2$ can only serve to increase the expected number of sensor activations, because $\E{X}$ is unchanged, and $\prob{X \ge 1}$ decreases. The latter is true essentially because $\prob{\exists i \in \set{1,2}: \sensor_i \text{ activates}} = 1 - (1-x_1)(1-x_2) = x - x_1x_2 < x$. To complete the proof, notice that repeating this process with $\sensor = \argmax (p_{\sensor})$ and $x_i = x/2$ ensures $X$ converges to a Poisson variable with mean $\alpha$, while only increasing $\E{X \ |\ X \ge 1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\E{X\mid X\ge1}=\E{X}/\prob{X\ge1}$, evaluate it in the Poisson limit, then show mass-splitting only increases it.

nodes.name: Proof that lazy renormalization samples correctly
nodes.statement: \begin{proof} Lazy renormalization selects each sensor $\sensor$ with probability $(1-e^{-\alpha})p_{\sensor}$, because of the way the random bits $r_{\sensor}$ are shared in order to implement a coupled distribution for sensor activation and selection. Note that it would be sufficient to run the \LimitProtocol on the correct (possibly oversampled) probabilities, $\alpha p_{\sensor}$, since then~\propref{thm:sampling} ensures that each $\sensor$ is selected with probability $(1 - e^{-\alpha}) p_{\sensor}$. The difficulty is that $\sensor$ does not have access to the correct normalizer $Z(t)$, but only its estimate (lower bound) for it, $Z_{\sensor}(t)$. To overcome this difficulty, we define a joint probability distribution over two random variables $(X_{\sensor}, Y_{\sensor})$, where \[ X_{\sensor} = X_{\sensor}(R) := \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1 & \text{if $R \ge 1 - \alpha \cdot\rho(w_{\sensor}(t), Z_{\sensor}(t))$} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{array} \right. \] \[ Y_{\sensor} = Y_{\sensor}(R) := \min \set{b \ :\ \sum_{a=0}^b \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^{a}}{a!} \ge R } \] and $\lambda := \alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\sensor}(t), Z(t))$, and $R$ is sampled uniformly at random from $[0,1]$. Now, note that $Y_{\sensor}$ is distributed as $\Poisson{\lambda}$. Also note that $Y_{\sensor} \ge 1$ implies $X_{\sensor} \ge 1$, because $Y_{\sensor} \ge 1$ implies $R \ge e^{-\lambda}$ and \[ e^{-\lambda} \ge 1 - \lambda \ge 1 - \alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\sensor}(t), Z_{\sensor}(t)) \] since $1 + x \le e^x$ for all $x \in \reals$, and $\rho(w_{\sensor}(t), Z_{\sensor}(t)) \ge \rho(w_{\sensor}(t), Z(t))$ due to fact that $Z_{\sensor}(t) \le Z(t)$. It follows that we can use the event $X_{\sensor} \ge 1$ as a conservative indicator that $\sensor$ should activate. In this case, it will send its sampled value for $R$, namely $r_{\sensor}$, and its weight $w_{\sensor}(t)$ to the server. The server knows $Z(t)$, and then can use $r_{\sensor}$ and $w_{\sensor}(t)$ to compute $Y_{\sensor}(r_{\sensor})$, the sample from $\Poisson{\lambda}$ that $\sensor$ would have drawn had it known $Z(t)$. The resulting distribution on selected sensors is thus exactly the same as in the \LimitProtocol without lazy renormalization. Invoking~\propref{thm:sampling} thus completes the proof. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Couple the activation indicator $X_{\sensor}$ and the Poisson variable $Y_{\sensor}$ through a shared uniform $R$, so the server can reconstruct the correct Poisson draw.

nodes.name: Proof of the lazy renormalization ratio theorem
nodes.statement: \begin{proof} Fix $\sensor$, and let $p(t) := p_{\sensor}(t)$, $q(t) := q_{\sensor}(t)$. We begin by bounding $\prob{q(t) \ge \lambda p(t)}$ for $\lambda \ge 1$. Let $t_0$ be the most recent round in which $q(t_0) = p(t_0)$. We assume $q(0) = p(0)$, so $t_0$ exists. Then $q(t) = p(t_0) \ge \lambda p(t)$ implies $p(t_0)/p(t) \ge \lambda$. By assumption $p(t')/p(t'+1) \le (1+\hat{\epsilon})$ for all $t'$, so $p(t_0)/p(t) \le (1+\hat{\epsilon})^{t-t_0}$. Thus $\lambda \le (1+\hat{\epsilon})^{t-t_0}$ and $t-t_0 \ge \ln(\lambda)/ \ln (1+\hat{\epsilon})$. Define $t(\lambda) := \ln(\lambda)/ \ln (1+\hat{\epsilon})$. By definition of $t_0$, there were no activations under lazy renormalization in rounds $t_0$ through $t-1$ inclusive, which occurs with probability $\prod_{t' = t_0}^{t-1} (1-\alpha q(t'))$ $=$ $(1-\alpha q(t))^{t-t_{0}} $ $\le$ $(1-\alpha q(t))^{\ceil{t(\lambda)}}$, where $\alpha$ is the oversampling parameter in the protocol. We now bound $\Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)}$. Recall that $\E{X} = \int_{x = 0}^{\infty} \prob{X \ge x}dx$ for any non-negative random variable $X$. It will also be convenient to define $\lamexp := \ln(1/(1 - \alpha q(t))) / \ln(1+\hat{\epsilon})$ and assume for now that $\lamexp > 1$. Conditioning on $q(t)$, we see that \[ \begin{array}{lcl} \vspace{2mm} \Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)} & = & \int_{\lambda = 0}^{\infty} \prob{q(t) \ge \lambda p(t)}d\lambda \\ \vspace{2mm} & = & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty} \prob{q(t) \ge \lambda p(t)}d\lambda \\ \vspace{2mm} & \le & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty} (1-\alpha q(t))^{t(\lambda)}d\lambda\\ \vspace{2mm} & = & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty} \lambda^{\ln(1-\alpha q(t))/\ln(1+\hat{\epsilon}) }d\lambda \\ \vspace{2mm} & = & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty} \lambda^{-\lamexp}d\lambda \\ \vspace{2mm} & = & 1 + \frac{1}{\lamexp - 1} \end{array} \] Using $\ln\paren{\frac{1}{1-x}} \ge x$ for all $x < 1$ and $\ln(1+x) \le x$ for all $x > -1$, we can show that $\lamexp \ge \alpha q(t)/\hat{\epsilon}$ so $1+\frac{1}{\lamexp - 1} \le \alpha q(t)/(\alpha q(t) - \hat{\epsilon})$. Thus, if $\alpha q(t) > \hat{\epsilon}$ then $\lamexp > 1$ and we obtain $\Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)} \le \alpha q(t)/(\alpha q(t) - \hat{\epsilon})$. If $q(t) >> \hat{\epsilon}$, this gives a good bound. If $q(t)$ is small, we rely on the assumption that $p(t) \ge \epsilon$ for all $t$ to get a trivial bound of $q(t)/p(t) \le q(t)/\epsilon$. We thus conclude \begin{equation} \Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)} \le \min \paren{\alpha q(t)/(\alpha q(t) - \hat{\epsilon}) ,\ q(t)/\epsilon}\mbox{.} \end{equation} Setting $q(t) = (\hat{\epsilon}/\alpha + \epsilon)$ to maximize this quantity yields an unconditional bound of $\E{q(t)/p(t)} \le 1 + \hat{\epsilon}/\alpha\epsilon$. To bound $\E{q(t)}$ in terms of $\E{p(t)}$, note that for all $q$ \begin{align*} q/\Econd{p(t)}{q(t)=q} & \le \Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)=q}\\ & \le 1 + \hat{\epsilon}/\alpha\epsilon \end{align*} where the first line is by Jensen's inequality, and the second is by equation~\ref{eqn:ratio-bound}. Thus $q \le \paren{1 + \hat{\epsilon}/\alpha\epsilon}\Econd{p(t)}{q(t)=q}$ for all $q$. Taking the expectation with respect to $q$ then proves $\E{q_{\sensor}(t)} \le \paren{1 + \frac{\hat{\epsilon}}{\alpha\epsilon}} \E{p_{\sensor}(t)}$ as claimed. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the tail $\prob{q(t)\ge\lambda p(t)}$ by the no-activation probability, integrate it, then combine with the trivial $q/\epsilon$ bound and apply Jensen.

nodes.name: Proof of the Distributed EXP3 activation bound
nodes.statement: \begin{proof}[of Theorem~~\ref{thm:dexp3-performance}.] We prove in Lemma~\ref{lem:exp3conditions} that \EXPthree satisfies the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:lazy_renorm_ratio} with $\epsilon = \gamma/\numsensors$ and $\hat{\epsilon} = (e-1)\frac{\gamma}{\numsensors}$. Thus by Theorem~\ref{thm:lazy_renorm_ratio} \begin{align*} \E{\sum_{\sensor} q_{\sensor}(t)} & \le \paren{1 + (e-1)/\alpha}\E{\sum_{\sensor} p_{\sensor}(t)}\\ & = \paren{1 + (e-1)/\alpha} \end{align*} because $\sum_{\sensor} p_{\sensor}(t) = 1$. Each sensor $\sensor$ activates with probability $\alpha q_{\sensor}(t)$, so the expected number of activations is \[ \E{\alpha \sum_{\sensor} q_{\sensor}(t)} \le \alpha\paren{1 + (e-1)/\alpha}\mbox{.} \] That proves the claimed bounds in expectation. To prove bounds with high probability, note that a sensor activates with probability $\alpha q_{\sensor}(t)$ in round $t$, where $q_{\sensor}(t)$ is a random variable. Fix $t$. Let $[\event]$ denote the indicator variable for the event $\event$, i.e., $[\event] = 1$ if $\event$ occurs, and $[\event] = 0$ otherwise. Then we can write $[\sensor \text{ activates in round }t] = [\alpha q_{\sensor}(t) \ge R]$, where $R$ is sampled uniformly at random from $[0,1]$ and $R$ is independent of $q_{\sensor}(t)$. Then if $f_R$ is the probability density functions of $R$ we can write \[ \begin{aligned} \prob{R \le \alpha q_{\sensor}(t)} & = \int_{r = 0}^1 \prob{\alpha q_{\sensor}(t) \ge R \ |\ R = r} f_R(r) dr\\ & = \int_{r = 0}^1 \prob{\alpha q_{\sensor}(t) \ge r} f_R(r) dr \\ & = \int_{r = 0}^1 \prob{\alpha q_{\sensor}(t) \ge r}dr \\ & = \E{ \alpha q_{\sensor}(t) } \end{aligned} \] Thus the number of sensor activations is a sum of $|\sensors|$ binary random variables with cumulative mean $\mu := \sum_{\sensor} \E{ \alpha q_{\sensor}(t) }$. We have already bounded this mean as $\mu \le \alpha + (e-1)$. From here a simple application of a Chernoff-Hoeffding bound suffices to prove that with high probability this sum is at most $\cO(\alpha + \log n)$. Let $A$ be the number of sensor activations. Then, e.g., Theorem~$5$ of~\cite{CL06} immediately implies \[ \prob{A \ge \mu(1 + \delta)} \le \exp \paren{ - \frac{\delta^2 \mu^2}{2 \mu + \frac{2\delta \mu}{3}}} \] For $\delta \ge 1$, this yields $\prob{A \ge \mu(1 + \delta)} \le \exp \paren{ - \frac{3\delta\mu}{8}}$. Setting $\delta = 1 + \frac{8c\ln n}{3\mu}$ ensures this probability is at most $n^{-c}$, hence $\prob{A \ge 2\mu + \frac{8}{3}c\ln n} \le n^{-c}$. Noting that $\mu \le \alpha + (e-1)$ completes the high probability bound on the number of activations. As for the number of messages, note that each message involves a sensor as sender or receiver, and by inspection the protocol only involves two messages per activated node. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the ratio theorem to bound the mean number of activations, then a Chernoff-Hoeffding bound for the high-probability version.

nodes.name: Proof of the always-selects corollary
nodes.statement: \begin{proof}[of Corollary~\ref{cor:dexp3-performance}.] Use the distributed \EXPthree protocol with lazy renormalization with $\alpha = \ln n$. We have already established that the probability of nothing being selected is $e^{-\alpha}$ or $1/n$ in this case. If nothing is selected, send out $n$ messages, one to each sensor, to rerun the protocol. The expected number of messages sent to initiate additional runs of the protocol is $\sum_{x=1}^{\infty} nx/n^{x} = \paren{1 - 1/n}^{-2} = 1 + \cO(1/n)$. Let $X$ be the number of sensor activations. As in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:broadcast-activations}, if $Y$ is the expected number of sensor activations without rerunning the protocol when nothing is selected, then $\E{X} = \E{Y}/\prob{Y \ge 1}$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:dexp3-performance} $\E{Y} \le \alpha\paren{1 + (e-1)/\alpha}$. Since $\prob{Y \ge 1} = 1 - e^{-\alpha}$, we conclude \[ \E{X} \le \ln n + (e-1) + \cO\paren{\frac{\ln n}{n}}\mbox{.} \] The with-high-probability bounds on the number of sensor activations are proved as in the proof of Corollary~\ref{cor:dexp3-performance}. As for the number of messages, note that other than messages sent to initiate additional runs of the protocol, there are only two messages per activated node. Finally, the regret bounds for distributed \EXPthree are the same as standard \EXPthree because by design the two algorithms select sensors from exactly the same distribution in each round. Note that the distribution in any given round is a random object depending on the algorithm's choices in the previous rounds, however on each round the distribution on distributions is the same for both \EXPthree variants, as can be readily proved by induction on the round number. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Set $\alpha=\ln n$, charge the reruns geometrically, and reuse $\E{X}=\E{Y}/\prob{Y\ge1}$; regret is unchanged since the selection distributions coincide.

nodes.name: Proof of the faulty-actions theorem
nodes.statement: \begin{proof} It suffices to prove the analogous result in the offline case; the ``meta-actions'' analysis in~\cite{streeter07tr} can then be used to complete the proof. So consider a set of elements $\sensors$ and the ``faulty'' versions $\sensors'$. Fix a monotone submodular $f:2^{\sensors} \to [0,1]$ and define $f'$ as above. Run the offline greedy algorithm on $f'$ to try to find the best set of $\K' = \frac{\K}{1-\delta}$ elements in $\sensors'$. Let $g'_i$ be the chosen element in stage $i$, and let $G'_i = \set{g'_j : 1 \le j \le i}$. Let $G_i$ denote the realization of $G'_i$ after sampling, so that $G_i \subseteq \set{g : g' \in G'_i}$. Let $S^* = \argmax_{S \subseteq \sensors, |S| \le \K}(f(S))$. We claim that for all $i$ \[ \Econd{f(G'_{i+1}) - f(G'_i)}{G_i} \ge \paren{1-\delta} \frac{f(S^*) - f(G_i)}{\K} \] because \begin{align*} f(S^*) - f(G_i) & \le f(G_i \cup S^*) - f(G_i)\\ & \le \sum_{\sensor \in S^*} \paren{f(G_i + \sensor) - f(G_i)}\\ & \le \K \cdot \max_{\sensor} \paren{f(G_i + \sensor) - f(G_i)} \end{align*} and $\max_{\sensor'} \paren{\Econd{f(G'_i + \sensor') - f(G'_i)}{G_i} }$ is at least equal to $(1-\delta)\max_{\sensor} \paren{f(G_i + \sensor) - f(G_i)}$. Removing the conditioning on $G_i$ we get \[ \E{f(G'_{i+1}) - f(G'_i)} \ge \paren{1-\delta}\frac{f(S^*) - \E{f(G'_i)}}{\K} \] Let $\Phi(i) = f(S^*) - \E{f(G'_{i})}$. The previous equation implies $\Phi(i+1) \le \Phi(i)\paren{1 - \frac{1-\delta}{\K}}$. By induction $\Phi(i) \le f(S^*)\paren{1 - \frac{1-\delta}{\K}}^i$. Using $1-x \le e^{-x}$ we conclude that $\Phi(\ceil{\K/(1-\delta)}) \le f(S^*)/e$ and $f'(G_{\K'}) \ge \paren{1-\frac{1}{e}}f(S^*)$. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the offline case, show each greedy stage closes a $(1-\delta)/\K$ fraction of the gap, and iterate the recursion by induction.

nodes.statement: \begin{proof}[Theorem~\ref{thm:better-lazydog}] To bound the number of sensor activations, we note there are $\K' := \ceil{\K/(1 - e^{-\alpha})}$ rounds, and each round activates at most $\alpha + (e-1)$ sensors in expectation and $\cO(\alpha + \log n)$ sensors with high probability by Theorem~\ref{thm:dexp3-performance} (which proves these bounds in the higher communication case where we do rerun the \LimitProtocolShort protocol if nothing is selected). In this case, it will send its sampled value for $R$, namely $r_{\sensor}$, and its weight $w_{\sensor}(t)$ to the server. The server knows $Z(t)$, and then can use $r_{\sensor}$ and $w_{\sensor}(t)$ to compute $Y_{\sensor}(r_{\sensor})$, the sample from $\Poisson{\lambda}$ that $\sensor$ would have drawn had it known $Z(t)$. The resulting distribution on selected sensors is thus exactly the same as in the \LimitProtocol without lazy renormalization. Invoking~\propref{thm:sampling} thus completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: From $r_{\sensor}$ and $w_{\sensor}(t)$ the server recovers $Y_{\sensor}$, so the selection law matches plain PMS.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Bound the tail $\prob{q(t)\ge\lambda p(t)}$ in rounds elapsed
nodes.statement: Fix $\sensor$, and let $p(t) := p_{\sensor}(t)$, $q(t) := q_{\sensor}(t)$. We begin by bounding $\prob{q(t) \ge \lambda p(t)}$ for $\lambda \ge 1$. Let $t_0$ be the most recent round in which $q(t_0) = p(t_0)$. We assume $q(0) = p(0)$, so $t_0$ exists. Then $q(t) = p(t_0) \ge \lambda p(t)$ implies $p(t_0)/p(t) \ge \lambda$. By assumption $p(t')/p(t'+1) \le (1+\hat{\epsilon})$ for all $t'$, so $p(t_0)/p(t) \le (1+\hat{\epsilon})^{t-t_0}$. Thus $\lambda \le (1+\hat{\epsilon})^{t-t_0}$ and $t-t_0 \ge \ln(\lambda)/ \ln (1+\hat{\epsilon})$. Define $t(\lambda) := \ln(\lambda)/ \ln (1+\hat{\epsilon})$.
nodes.statement_short: An overestimate by a factor $\lambda$ forces at least $t(\lambda)=\ln\lambda/\ln(1+\hat{\epsilon})$ silent rounds.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Silent rounds have probability $(1-\alpha q(t))^{t-t_0}$
nodes.statement: By definition of $t_0$, there were no activations under lazy renormalization in rounds $t_0$ through $t-1$ inclusive, which occurs with probability $\prod_{t' = t_0}^{t-1} (1-\alpha q(t'))$ $=$ $(1-\alpha q(t))^{t-t_{0}} $ $\le$ $(1-\alpha q(t))^{\ceil{t(\lambda)}}$, where $\alpha$ is the oversampling parameter in the protocol.
nodes.statement_short: No activation between $t_0$ and $t-1$ has probability at most $(1-\alpha q(t))^{\ceil{t(\lambda)}}$.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Integrate the tail bound
nodes.statement: We now bound $\Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)}$. Recall that $\E{X} = \int_{x = 0}^{\infty} \prob{X \ge x}dx$ for any non-negative random variable $X$. It will also be convenient to define $\lamexp := \ln(1/(1 - \alpha q(t))) / \ln(1+\hat{\epsilon})$ and assume for now that $\lamexp > 1$. Conditioning on $q(t)$, we see that \[ \begin{array}{lcl} \vspace{2mm} \Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)} & = & \int_{\lambda = 0}^{\infty} \prob{q(t) \ge \lambda p(t)}d\lambda \\ \vspace{2mm} & = & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty} \prob{q(t) \ge \lambda p(t)}d\lambda \\ \vspace{2mm} & \le & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty} (1-\alpha q(t))^{t(\lambda)}d\lambda\\ \vspace{2mm} & = & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty} \lambda^{\ln(1-\alpha q(t))/\ln(1+\hat{\epsilon}) }d\lambda \\ \vspace{2mm} & = & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty} \lambda^{-\lamexp}d\lambda \\ \vspace{2mm} & = & 1 + \frac{1}{\lamexp - 1} \end{array} \]
nodes.statement_short: Using $\E{X}=\int\prob{X\ge x}dx$, the integral collapses to $1+1/(\lamexp-1)$.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Convert the exponent bound into a ratio bound
nodes.statement: Using $\ln\paren{\frac{1}{1-x}} \ge x$ for all $x < 1$ and $\ln(1+x) \le x$ for all $x > -1$, we can show that $\lamexp \ge \alpha q(t)/\hat{\epsilon}$ so $1+\frac{1}{\lamexp - 1} \le \alpha q(t)/(\alpha q(t) - \hat{\epsilon})$.
nodes.statement_short: Logarithm inequalities give $\lamexp\ge\alpha q(t)/\hat{\epsilon}$, hence the multiplicative bound.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Combine with the trivial bound for small $q(t)$
nodes.statement: If $q(t) >> \hat{\epsilon}$, this gives a good bound. If $q(t)$ is small, we rely on the assumption that $p(t) \ge \epsilon$ for all $t$ to get a trivial bound of $q(t)/p(t) \le q(t)/\epsilon$. We thus conclude \begin{equation} \Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)} \le \min \paren{\alpha q(t)/(\alpha q(t) - \hat{\epsilon}) ,\ q(t)/\epsilon}\mbox{.} \end{equation} Setting $q(t) = (\hat{\epsilon}/\alpha + \epsilon)$ to maximize this quantity yields an unconditional bound of $\E{q(t)/p(t)} \le 1 + \hat{\epsilon}/\alpha\epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Taking the minimum of the two regimes and maximizing over $q(t)$ yields the unconditional bound.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Transfer the bound to $\E{q(t)}$ via Jensen
nodes.statement: To bound $\E{q(t)}$ in terms of $\E{p(t)}$, note that for all $q$ \begin{align*} q/\Econd{p(t)}{q(t)=q} & \le \Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)=q}\\ & \le 1 + \hat{\epsilon}/\alpha\epsilon \end{align*} where the first line is by Jensen's inequality, and the second is by equation~\ref{eqn:ratio-bound}. Thus $q \le \paren{1 + \hat{\epsilon}/\alpha\epsilon}\Econd{p(t)}{q(t)=q}$ for all $q$. Taking the expectation with respect to $q$ then proves $\E{q_{\sensor}(t)} \le \paren{1 + \frac{\hat{\epsilon}}{\alpha\epsilon}} \E{p_{\sensor}(t)}$ as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Jensen plus the ratio bound gives $\E{q_{\sensor}(t)}\le(1+\hat{\epsilon}/\alpha\epsilon)\E{p_{\sensor}(t)}$.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Reduce to the weight-growth factor
nodes.statement: The former equality is an easy observation. To prove the latter equality, fix a round $t$ and a selected action $\sensor$. Let $w_{\sensor}(t)$ be the weight of $\sensor$ in round $t$, and $W(t)$ be the total weight of all actions in round $t$. Let $\payoff$ be the payoff to $\sensor$ in round $t$. Given the update rule $w_{\sensor}(t+1) = w_{\sensor}(t)\exp\paren{\frac{\gamma}{\numsensors}\frac{\payoff(\sensor,t)}{p_{\sensor}(t)}}$, only the probabilities of the other actions will be decreased. It is not hard to see that they will be decreased by a multiplicative factor of at most $W(t)/W(t+1)$, no matter what the learning parameter $\gamma$ is.
nodes.statement_short: Other actions' probabilities shrink by at most the total-weight growth factor $W(t)/W(t+1)$.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Write the total weight after the update
nodes.statement: By the update rule, \[ W(t+1) = W(t) + w_{\sensor}(t)\paren{\exp\paren{\frac{\gamma}{\numsensors} \frac{\payoff}{p_{\sensor}(t)}} - 1}\mbox{.} \]
nodes.statement_short: Only the selected action's weight changes, so $W(t+1)=W(t)+w_{\sensor}(t)(e^{\cdot}-1)$.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Bound the growth ratio using $e^x\le1+x+(e-2)x^2$
nodes.statement: Let $p := p_{\sensor}(t)$ and $x := \frac{\gamma}{\numsensors}\payoff$. Dividing the above equation by $W(t)$, we get \begin{align} \frac{W(t+1)}{W(t)} & = 1 + p\paren{\exp\paren{x/p} - 1} \\ & \le 1 + p\paren{x/p + (e-2)(x/p)^2}\\ & \le 1 + x + (e-2)x^2/p \end{align} where in the second line we have used $e^x \le 1 + x + (e-2)x^2$ for $x \in [0,1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Substituting $p$ and $x$ and applying the quadratic exponential bound gives $1+x+(e-2)x^2/p$.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Conclude the value of $\hat{\epsilon}$
nodes.statement: Note $\payoff \le 1$ implies $x \le \gamma/n \le p$, so $\frac{W(t+1)}{W(t)} \le 1 + (e-1)x \le 1 + (e-1)\frac{\gamma}{\numsensors}$. It follows that setting $\hat{\epsilon} = (e-1)\frac{\gamma}{\numsensors}$ is sufficient to ensure $p_{\sensor}(t+1) \ge p_{\sensor}(t)/(1+\hat{\epsilon})$ for all $t$. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Since $x\le\gamma/n\le p$, the ratio is at most $1+(e-1)\gamma/n$, giving $\hat{\epsilon}$.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Apply the lemma and the ratio theorem
nodes.statement: We prove in Lemma~\ref{lem:exp3conditions} that \EXPthree satisfies the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:lazy_renorm_ratio} with $\epsilon = \gamma/\numsensors$ and $\hat{\epsilon} = (e-1)\frac{\gamma}{\numsensors}$. Thus by Theorem~\ref{thm:lazy_renorm_ratio} \begin{align*} \E{\sum_{\sensor} q_{\sensor}(t)} & \le \paren{1 + (e-1)/\alpha}\E{\sum_{\sensor} p_{\sensor}(t)}\\ & = \paren{1 + (e-1)/\alpha} \end{align*} because $\sum_{\sensor} p_{\sensor}(t) = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: EXP3 meets the assumptions, so $\E{\sum_{\sensor}q_{\sensor}(t)}\le 1+(e-1)/\alpha$.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Turn the probability bound into an activation bound
nodes.statement: Each sensor $\sensor$ activates with probability $\alpha q_{\sensor}(t)$, so the expected number of activations is \[ \E{\alpha \sum_{\sensor} q_{\sensor}(t)} \le \alpha\paren{1 + (e-1)/\alpha}\mbox{.} \] That proves the claimed bounds in expectation.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplying by $\alpha$ gives at most $\alpha+(e-1)$ expected activations.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Rewrite activation as a comparison with an independent uniform
nodes.statement: To prove bounds with high probability, note that a sensor activates with probability $\alpha q_{\sensor}(t)$ in round $t$, where $q_{\sensor}(t)$ is a random variable. Fix $t$. Let $[\event]$ denote the indicator variable for the event $\event$, i.e., $[\event] = 1$ if $\event$ occurs, and $[\event] = 0$ otherwise. Then we can write $[\sensor \text{ activates in round }t] = [\alpha q_{\sensor}(t) \ge R]$, where $R$ is sampled uniformly at random from $[0,1]$ and $R$ is independent of $q_{\sensor}(t)$. Then if $f_R$ is the probability density functions of $R$ we can write \[ \begin{aligned} \prob{R \le \alpha q_{\sensor}(t)} & = \int_{r = 0}^1 \prob{\alpha q_{\sensor}(t) \ge R \ |\ R = r} f_R(r) dr\\ & = \int_{r = 0}^1 \prob{\alpha q_{\sensor}(t) \ge r} f_R(r) dr \\ & = \int_{r = 0}^1 \prob{\alpha q_{\sensor}(t) \ge r}dr \\ & = \E{ \alpha q_{\sensor}(t) } \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Express the activation indicator as $[\alpha q_{\sensor}(t)\ge R]$ with $R$ uniform and independent.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Apply a Chernoff-Hoeffding bound
nodes.statement: Thus the number of sensor activations is a sum of $|\sensors|$ binary random variables with cumulative mean $\mu := \sum_{\sensor} \E{ \alpha q_{\sensor}(t) }$. We have already bounded this mean as $\mu \le \alpha + (e-1)$. From here a simple application of a Chernoff-Hoeffding bound suffices to prove that with high probability this sum is at most $\cO(\alpha + \log n)$. Let $A$ be the number of sensor activations. Then, e.g., Theorem~$5$ of~\cite{CL06} immediately implies \[ \prob{A \ge \mu(1 + \delta)} \le \exp \paren{ - \frac{\delta^2 \mu^2}{2 \mu + \frac{2\delta \mu}{3}}} \] For $\delta \ge 1$, this yields $\prob{A \ge \mu(1 + \delta)} \le \exp \paren{ - \frac{3\delta\mu}{8}}$. Setting $\delta = 1 + \frac{8c\ln n}{3\mu}$ ensures this probability is at most $n^{-c}$, hence $\prob{A \ge 2\mu + \frac{8}{3}c\ln n} \le n^{-c}$. Noting that $\mu \le \alpha + (e-1)$ completes the high probability bound on the number of activations.
nodes.statement_short: A Chernoff-Hoeffding tail with $\delta=1+8c\ln n/(3\mu)$ gives $\cO(\alpha+\log n)$ whp.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Count the messages
nodes.statement: As for the number of messages, note that each message involves a sensor as sender or receiver, and by inspection the protocol only involves two messages per activated node.
nodes.statement_short: Inspection of the protocol shows two messages per activated node.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Set the oversampling parameter to $\ln n$
nodes.statement: Use the distributed \EXPthree protocol with lazy renormalization with $\alpha = \ln n$. We have already established that the probability of nothing being selected is $e^{-\alpha}$ or $1/n$ in this case.
nodes.statement_short: With $\alpha=\ln n$ the probability of an empty round is $1/n$.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Charge the rerun messages
nodes.statement: If nothing is selected, send out $n$ messages, one to each sensor, to rerun the protocol. The expected number of messages sent to initiate additional runs of the protocol is $\sum_{x=1}^{\infty} nx/n^{x} = \paren{1 - 1/n}^{-2} = 1 + \cO(1/n)$.
nodes.statement_short: The geometric series of rerun broadcasts costs only $1+\cO(1/n)$ messages in expectation.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Reuse the conditioning identity for activations
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be the number of sensor activations. As in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:broadcast-activations}, if $Y$ is the expected number of sensor activations without rerunning the protocol when nothing is selected, then $\E{X} = \E{Y}/\prob{Y \ge 1}$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:dexp3-performance} $\E{Y} \le \alpha\paren{1 + (e-1)/\alpha}$. Since $\prob{Y \ge 1} = 1 - e^{-\alpha}$, we conclude \[ \E{X} \le \ln n + (e-1) + \cO\paren{\frac{\ln n}{n}}\mbox{.} \]
nodes.statement_short: $\E{X}=\E{Y}/\prob{Y\ge1}$ with the Theorem's bound yields $\ln n+(e-1)+\cO(\ln n/n)$.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: High-probability bound and message count
nodes.statement: The with-high-probability bounds on the number of sensor activations are proved as in the proof of Corollary~\ref{cor:dexp3-performance}. As for the number of messages, note that other than messages sent to initiate additional runs of the protocol, there are only two messages per activated node.
nodes.statement_short: The whp bound is as before and, apart from reruns, there are two messages per activation.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Regret is unchanged
nodes.statement: Finally, the regret bounds for distributed \EXPthree are the same as standard \EXPthree because by design the two algorithms select sensors from exactly the same distribution in each round. Note that the distribution in any given round is a random object depending on the algorithm's choices in the previous rounds, however on each round the distribution on distributions is the same for both \EXPthree variants, as can be readily proved by induction on the round number.
nodes.statement_short: Both variants induce the same round-by-round distribution, provable by induction on the round.
nodes.section: B Results in the Star Network Model

nodes.name: Reduce to the offline case
nodes.statement: It suffices to prove the analogous result in the offline case; the ``meta-actions'' analysis in~\cite{streeter07tr} can then be used to complete the proof.
nodes.statement_short: The meta-actions analysis of Streeter & Golovin lifts an offline statement to the online one.
nodes.section: C Algorithm OG_unit with Faulty Actions

nodes.name: Run greedy on the faulty ground set
nodes.statement: So consider a set of elements $\sensors$ and the ``faulty'' versions $\sensors'$. Fix a monotone submodular $f:2^{\sensors} \to [0,1]$ and define $f'$ as above. Run the offline greedy algorithm on $f'$ to try to find the best set of $\K' = \frac{\K}{1-\delta}$ elements in $\sensors'$. Let $g'_i$ be the chosen element in stage $i$, and let $G'_i = \set{g'_j : 1 \le j \le i}$. Let $G_i$ denote the realization of $G'_i$ after sampling, so that $G_i \subseteq \set{g : g' \in G'_i}$. Let $S^* = \argmax_{S \subseteq \sensors, |S| \le \K}(f(S))$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the greedy picks $G'_i$, their realizations $G_i$, and the offline optimum $S^*$.
nodes.section: C Algorithm OG_unit with Faulty Actions

nodes.name: Claim the per-stage progress inequality
nodes.statement: We claim that for all $i$ \[ \Econd{f(G'_{i+1}) - f(G'_i)}{G_i} \ge \paren{1-\delta} \frac{f(S^*) - f(G_i)}{\K} \]
nodes.statement_short: Each stage closes at least a $(1-\delta)/\K$ fraction of the remaining gap in expectation.
nodes.section: C Algorithm OG_unit with Faulty Actions

nodes.name: Justify it by submodularity and the failure probability
nodes.statement: because \begin{align*} f(S^*) - f(G_i) & \le f(G_i \cup S^*) - f(G_i)\\ & \le \sum_{\sensor \in S^*} \paren{f(G_i + \sensor) - f(G_i)}\\ & \le \K \cdot \max_{\sensor} \paren{f(G_i + \sensor) - f(G_i)} \end{align*} and $\max_{\sensor'} \paren{\Econd{f(G'_i + \sensor') - f(G'_i)}{G_i} }$ is at least equal to $(1-\delta)\max_{\sensor} \paren{f(G_i + \sensor) - f(G_i)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Submodularity bounds the gap by $\K$ times the best marginal, which faulty elements retain up to $(1-\delta)$.
nodes.section: C Algorithm OG_unit with Faulty Actions

nodes.name: Solve the recursion by induction
nodes.statement: Removing the conditioning on $G_i$ we get \[ \E{f(G'_{i+1}) - f(G'_i)} \ge \paren{1-\delta}\frac{f(S^*) - \E{f(G'_i)}}{\K} \] Let $\Phi(i) = f(S^*) - \E{f(G'_{i})}$. The previous equation implies $\Phi(i+1) \le \Phi(i)\paren{1 - \frac{1-\delta}{\K}}$. By induction $\Phi(i) \le f(S^*)\paren{1 - \frac{1-\delta}{\K}}^i$. Using $1-x \le e^{-x}$ we conclude that $\Phi(\ceil{\K/(1-\delta)}) \le f(S^*)/e$ and $f'(G_{\K'}) \ge \paren{1-\frac{1}{e}}f(S^*)$.
nodes.statement_short: The gap contracts by $(1-(1-\delta)/\K)$ per stage, so after $\ceil{\K/(1-\delta)}$ stages it is at most $f(S^*)/e$.
nodes.section: C Algorithm OG_unit with Faulty Actions

nodes.name: Bound the number of activations
nodes.statement: To bound the number of sensor activations, we note there are $\K' := \ceil{\K/(1 - e^{-\alpha})}$ rounds, and each round activates at most $\alpha + (e-1)$ sensors in expectation and $\cO(\alpha + \log n)$ sensors with high probability by Theorem~\ref{thm:dexp3-performance} (which proves these bounds in the higher communication case where we do rerun the \LimitProtocolShort protocol if nothing is selected). This, and the fact that $\alpha/(1 - e^{-\alpha}) = O(\alpha)$ for $\alpha > 0$ yields the claimed activation bounds.
nodes.statement_short: Over $\K'$ stages the per-stage bounds of the Distributed EXP3 theorem give the claimed totals.
nodes.section: C Algorithm OG_unit with Faulty Actions

nodes.name: Messages are at most twice the activations
nodes.statement: It is an easy observation that the number of messages is at most twice the number of activations.
nodes.statement_short: Each activation involves at most two messages.
nodes.section: C Algorithm OG_unit with Faulty Actions

nodes.name: At most $\K'$ sensors are selected per round
nodes.statement: Clearly, at most one sensor per stage is activated, so at most $\K'$ are activated over one round.
nodes.statement_short: One selection per stage caps the round's selections at $\K'$.
nodes.section: C Algorithm OG_unit with Faulty Actions

nodes.name: Regret follows from the faulty-actions theorem
nodes.statement: Finally, the regret bound follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:faulty-sensors}, using $\delta = e^{-\alpha}$.
nodes.statement_short: Instantiate the faulty-actions theorem with failure probability $\delta=e^{-\alpha}$.
nodes.section: C Algorithm OG_unit with Faulty Actions

nodes.name: Start from the empty set
nodes.statement: starts with the empty set $\cA_{0}=\emptyset$
nodes.statement_short: Initialize the selected set to $\emptyset$.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Offline Sensor Selection Problem

nodes.name: Add the element of maximal marginal gain
nodes.statement: and iteratively adds the element $$s_{k}=\argmax_{s\in\sensors\setminus \cA_{k-1}} f(\cA_{k-1}\cup\{s\});\ \ \cA_{k}=\cA_{k-1}\cup\{s_{k}\}$$
nodes.statement_short: Repeatedly append the sensor maximizing $f(\cA_{k-1}\cup\{s\})$.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Offline Sensor Selection Problem

nodes.name: Initialize the arm weights
nodes.statement: It maintains a set of weights $w_{s}$, one for each arm (sensor) $s$, initialized to 1.
nodes.statement_short: Set every arm's weight to $1$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Centralized Online Single Sensor Selection

nodes.name: Sample an arm from the $\gamma$-mixed weight distribution
nodes.statement: At every round $t$, it will select each arm $s$ with probability $$p_{s}=(1-\gamma)\frac{w_{s}}{\sum_{s'} w_{s'}}+\frac{\gamma}{\numsensors},$$
nodes.statement_short: Draw an arm with probability mixing weight-proportional exploitation and uniform exploration.
nodes.section: 3.1 Centralized Online Single Sensor Selection

nodes.name: Update the selected arm's weight
nodes.statement: Once an arm $s$ has been selected, a feedback $r=\obj_{t}(\{s\})$ is obtained, and the weight $w_{s}$ is updated to $$w_{s}\leftarrow w_{s}\exp(\eta r/p_{s}).$$
nodes.statement_short: Multiply the chosen arm's weight by $\exp(\eta r/p_s)$ using the importance-weighted reward.
nodes.section: 3.1 Centralized Online Single Sensor Selection

nodes.name: Initialize $\K$ bandit algorithms
nodes.statement: Initialize $\K$ multiarmed bandit algorithms $\Alg_1, \Alg_2, \ldots, \Alg_\K$,\\ \hspace{0cm} each with action set $\sensors$.\\
nodes.statement_short: Create one bandit instance per greedy stage, all over the sensor set.
nodes.section: 3.2 Centralized Selection of Multiple Sensors

nodes.name: Loop over rounds
nodes.statement: For each round $t \in [T]$\\
nodes.statement_short: Iterate over rounds.
nodes.section: 3.2 Centralized Selection of Multiple Sensors

nodes.name: Loop over stages in parallel
nodes.statement: For each stage $i \in [\K]$ in parallel\\
nodes.statement_short: Stages run in parallel.
nodes.section: 3.2 Centralized Selection of Multiple Sensors

nodes.name: Each bandit picks an action
nodes.statement: $\Alg_i$ selects an action $\sensor^t_i$\\
nodes.statement_short: Bandit $i$ picks a sensor.
nodes.section: 3.2 Centralized Selection of Multiple Sensors

nodes.name: Feed back the incremental benefit
nodes.statement: For each $i \in [\K]$ in parallel\\ \hspace{0.6cm} feedback $\obj_t(\set{\sensor^t_j : j \le i }) - \obj_t(\set{\sensor^t_j : j < i })$ to $\Alg_i$.\\
nodes.statement_short: Return to each bandit the marginal utility its own pick contributed.
nodes.section: 3.2 Centralized Selection of Multiple Sensors

nodes.name: Output the selected set
nodes.statement: Output $S_t = \set{a^t_1, a^t_2, \ldots, a^t_\K}$.\\
nodes.statement_short: Emit the union of the stages' picks as $S_t$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Centralized Selection of Multiple Sensors

nodes.name: Broadcast one uniform and activate by CDF interval
nodes.statement: A naive distributed algorithm would be to let each sensor keep track of all activation probabilities $p$. Then, one sensor (e.g., with the lowest identifier) would broadcast a single random number $u$ uniformly distributed in $[0,1]$, and the sensor $\sensor$ for which $\sum_{i=1}^{\sensor-1} p_{i} \le u < \sum_{i=1}^{\sensor} p_{i}$ would activate.
nodes.statement_short: One sensor broadcasts $u\sim U[0,1]$ and the sensor whose cumulative interval contains $u$ activates.
nodes.section: 4.1 Distributed Selection of a Single Sensor

nodes.name: Local-storage variant: broadcast masses in ID order
nodes.statement: Instead, each sensor $\sensor$ could store only their own probability mass $p_{\sensor}$; the sensors would then, in order of their identifiers, broadcast their probabilities $p_{\sensor}$, and stop once the sum of the probabilities exceeds $u$.
nodes.statement_short: Sensors announce their own masses in ID order and stop once the running sum passes $u$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Distributed Selection of a Single Sensor

nodes.name: Each sensor acts in parallel
nodes.statement: For each sensor $\sensor$ in parallel
nodes.statement_short: All sensors act in parallel.
nodes.section: 4.1 Distributed Selection of a Single Sensor

nodes.name: Draw a Bernoulli activation variable
nodes.statement: Sample $X_{\sensor} \sim \Bernoulli{p_{\sensor}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Toss a coin of bias $p_{\sensor}$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Distributed Selection of a Single Sensor

nodes.name: Activate on a positive draw
nodes.statement: If $(X_{\sensor} = 1)$, $X_{\sensor}$ activates.
nodes.statement_short: Activate exactly when the coin comes up heads.
nodes.section: 4.1 Distributed Selection of a Single Sensor

nodes.name: Elect one active sensor uniformly at random
nodes.statement: All active sensors $S$ coordinate to select a single sensor uniformly at random from $S$, e.g., by electing the minimum ID sensor in $S$ to do the sampling.
nodes.statement_short: The active set picks one of its members uniformly, coordinated by the minimum-ID sensor.
nodes.section: 4.1 Distributed Selection of a Single Sensor

nodes.name: Each sensor acts in parallel
nodes.statement: For each sensor $\sensor$ in parallel
nodes.statement_short: All sensors act in parallel.
nodes.section: 4.1 Distributed Selection of a Single Sensor

nodes.name: Draw a binomial count
nodes.statement: Sample $X_{\sensor} \sim \Binomial{\ceil{N \cdot p_{\sensor}}, 1/N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Draw the fictitious-copy count.
nodes.section: 4.1 Distributed Selection of a Single Sensor

nodes.name: Activate on a positive count
nodes.statement: If $(X_{\sensor} \ge 1)$, then activate sensor $\sensor$.
nodes.statement_short: Activate whenever at least one fictitious copy fired.
nodes.section: 4.1 Distributed Selection of a Single Sensor

nodes.name: Select proportionally to the counts
nodes.statement: From the active sensors $S$, select sensor $\sensor$ with probability $X_{\sensor}/\sum_{\sensor'\in S} X_{\sensor'}$.\\
nodes.statement_short: Choose among active sensors with probability proportional to their drawn counts.
nodes.section: 4.1 Distributed Selection of a Single Sensor

nodes.name: Initialize weights and normalizers
nodes.statement: Initialize $w_{\sensor, i} \gets 1$ and $Z_{\sensor,i} \gets |\sensors|$ for all $\sensor \in \sensors$, $i \in [\K]$.
nodes.statement_short: Every sensor sets all stage weights to $1$ and all normalizers to $|\sensors|$.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Distributed Online Greedy Algorithm
